Commentary.Commentary: We are back for the chase! The Australian players are heading out to the middle and spreading to take up their respective field positions. The Indian openers - Rohit Sharma and Shubman Gill walk out to a huge roar. Mitchell Starc has the new ball in his hand and is raring to go. Here we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Right then, 237 is the target for India to avoid a whitewash. The crowd has turned up in big numbers, hoping to watch Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma in action - possibly for the last time for the former in Australia. The visitors will back themselves to chase this down, but it could take just one fiery spell from Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc, or even some magic from Adam Zampa to turn things around. India might hold a slight edge, but nothing is guaranteed here. They’ll need to stay sharp and not take the Aussies lightly. Join us in a bit for the second essay.

India will be delighted with how things turned out with the ball after being put in to field. Mohammed Siraj and Harshit Rana were a touch inconsistent with the new ball, allowing the Aussies to get off to a good start, but Siraj drew first blood in the 10th over. Axar Patel then struck right after the first drinks break, removing Mitchell Marsh. . There was a phase where wickets dried up - Prasidh Krishna even put down a catch, and things seemed to be slipping away. However, Washington Sundar stepped up to break the stand and bowled a tidy 10-over spell on the trot. From there, India regained control. Rana’s second spell was outstanding, as once he dismissed Alex Carey, the tide turned completely. He went on to claim four wickets, while Kuldeep Yadav and Prasidh Krishna chipped in with one apiece to restrict Australia to a below-par total.

It was an innings of two halves for Australia. The openers got off to a bright start, both looking assured at the crease as they added 61 before Travis Head was dismissed. Mitchell Marsh couldn’t carry on for long either, falling for 41. The Aussies then had to rebuild, and Matt Renshaw did that smartly, first with Matthew Short, rotating the strike well and finding the occasional boundary, notching up a fine fifty, then with Alex Carey, who took his time to settle in. The pair stitched together a valuable stand of over 50 runs and laid what looked like a solid platform. However, once Carey departed, things unraveled quickly - the middle order failed to make any real contribution as they slumped from 183/3 to 201/7. The lower order tried to chip in, with Cooper Connolly and Nathan Ellis adding some handy runs, but it wasn’t enough to take them anywhere close to a par score on this ground.

A superb bowling effort from India! After being on the back foot in the first couple of games, they’ve bounced back strongly here and given themselves a real chance to finish the series on a high. Australia, on the other hand, will be disappointed - after the start they got, they’d certainly feel there were a lot more runs left out there.

Commentary.Commentary: All set for action to get underway at the historic SCG. It is almost a full house as the Indians spread out of the team huddle and take their respective fielding positions. Travis Head and Mitchell Marsh are the two openers for Australia. And it will be Mohammed Siraj to get us underway with the first over. 'The Bison' to face. Two slips in place. Here we go...

UPDATE - Nitish Kumar Reddy picked up a left quadricep injury during the second ODI in Adelaide, which ruled him out of the 3rd and final ODI in Sydney. He is being monitored on a daily basis, according to the BCCI medical team.

The captain of India, Shubman Gill, says that they would have bowled first, so they got what they wanted. Adds that they want to hit the good lengths, restrict the Aussies and then chase it down. Mentions that they had enough runs in the last game but just missed a couple of chances and couldn't get over the line. Informs that they have made a couple of changes - Kuldeep Yadav and Prasidh Krishna come in for Nitish Kumar Reddy and Arshdeep Singh.

The captain of Australia, Mitchell Marsh, says it looks like a really nice wicket and a nice day in Sydney. He hopes to put on a very good total. Mentions that the way the young guys like Mitchell Owen and Cooper Connolly stepped up in the previous game was fabulous to see. Adds that Connolly is a calm character and played fabulously. Calls it a great sign for their side, and that it's about winning games in different types of ways to become one of the best teams in the world. Says it is a great opportunity for them to go 3-0 up. Informs that Nathan Ellis is back in the side for Xavier Bartlett.

India (Playing XI) - Shubman Gill (C), Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Shreyas Iyer, Axar Patel, KL Rahul (WK), Washington Sundar, Harshit Rana, Kuldeep Yadav (In place of Nitish Kumar Reddy), Prasidh Krishna (In place of Arshdeep Singh), Mohammed Siraj.

Australia (Playing XI) - Mitchell Marsh (C), Travis Head, Matthew Short, Matt Renshaw, Alex Carey (WK), Cooper Connolly, Mitchell Owen, Mitchell Starc, Adam Zampa, Nathan Ellis (In place of Xavier Bartlett), Josh Hazlewood.
TOSS - The coin lands in favour of Mitchell Marsh and Australia have elected to BAT first. With this, India have now lost 18 tosses in a row since the 2023 ODI World Cup - Unbelievable stat!

PITCH REPORT - Parthiv Patel and Shane Watson provide their analysis from pitchside. Watson notes the pitch is quite hard and firm, with patches of green grass visible on the surface. Also observes a lot of cracks that run down vertically and says that the quicks would like to line a few up. He suggests the fast bowlers could find some movement in the early stages. But also mentions that at SCG, the ball goes through nicely, so he believes that there will be a lot of value for the shots here due to good pace and bounce. He considers it a venue conducive to high scores and highlights that it has historically been a high scoring ground. Parthiv concurs, adding that this appears to be the most batter-friendly surface of the series thus far and concludes by saying that it will be a very good contest.

Ahead of the series, all eyes were on the return of Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli to international cricket after the Champions Trophy, but things haven’t quite gone according to script. Rohit did show glimpses of his class with a fluent 73, but Kohli’s twin failures have raised concerns. He’ll be desperate to find some form in this final ODI. On the brighter side, Shreyas Iyer has looked assured in the middle, while Axar Patel’s all-round contributions and KL Rahul’s composure have added some balance. The bowling, however, has lacked consistency - Harshit Rana’s inclusion has come under scrutiny, and both Mohammed Siraj and Arshdeep Singh will need to hit their stride quickly. Kuldeep Yadav, who’s been warming the bench so far, could well get a chance here to make an impact and help India finish the series on a high. Stay tuned for toss and other updates.

Australia have once again shown why they’re nearly unbeatable in their own backyard. Mitchell Marsh has led the side with confidence in Pat Cummins’ absence, and his leadership has been reflected in the team’s dominant displays. The opening game highlighted their incredible bench strength as they dismantled India’s batting lineup with clinical precision. Josh Hazlewood has been his consistent self, while Xavier Bartlett’s emergence and Adam Zampa’s control in the middle overs have been big positives. In the second ODI, they were briefly tested, but composed half-centuries from Matthew Short and Cooper Connolly ensured another fantastic win. With the series already in the bag, the hosts might use this final match to rotate a few players and give opportunities to some of their fringe talents.

Hello and welcome, folks! After the action in Perth and Adelaide, the series now moves to the iconic Sydney Cricket Ground for the third and final ODI. Australia have already sealed the series with two commanding performances and will be eyeing a clean sweep to finish in style. India, on the other hand, will be playing for pride and will hope to end the series on a positive note by giving their fans something to smile about.

When the storm passes, only the strongest trees remain - that quote from Seneca might just fit perfectly for this India vs Australia showdown. After back-to-back wins, the Aussies are cruising 2-0 in this ODI series, while India are hanging by the thread of pride. Now, as we land in Sydney for the final ODI, the big question looms - will Australia sweep, or will India finally roar back? What a tour this has turned out to be! It began with hope, hype, and a hint of nostalgia - Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli returning to international cricket after a seven-month hiatus. The spotlight was hot, the anticipation hotter. But two matches in, and the story’s taken a turn - Australia flying high, India scratching their heads. Perth’s rain-soaked mess left India bruised at 136/9, and Adelaide… well, heartbreak again. Despite Rohit’s elegant 73 and Iyer’s fluent fifty, Adam Zampa spun a web too tricky to escape. So, what’s gone wrong for India? Or maybe the better question - what hasn’t? In Perth, the top order collapsed faster than a deck of cards in a cyclone. Kohli’s golden duck - ouch! Then Adelaide brought promise, where Rohit timed like old times, Iyer and Axar steadied the ship, and Harshit Rana swung late. Yet, even 264 wasn’t enough as the bowlers struggled to land that killer blow. Now, at 0-2 down, pride is all that’s left to play for. But sometimes, pride is the most dangerous motivator, isn’t it? Oh, the phenomenon - Rohit and Kohli - the two icons everyone came to watch! Rohit looked back in rhythm, punching through covers with that lazy elegance only he can pull off. Kohli, though, couldn’t find his groove - out for ducks in both games, yet when he walked off at Adelaide, he raised his gloves to the crowd. Was that a silent goodbye to his beloved Adelaide - the ground where he’s crafted so many memories across three formats? Both men, now ODI specialists, stand at a crossroad. Will they be India’s guiding light to the 2027 ODI World Cup? Or is this the slow sunset of an era? Australia, meanwhile, have been everything India weren’t - ruthless, balanced, and clinical. Mitchell Marsh’s leadership has been calm yet lethal. Matthew Short’s 74 and young Connolly’s 61 in Adelaide sealed the deal with authority, while Zampa’s four-fer reminded everyone why he’s world-class. Even their newcomers, Bartlett and Owen, have made an instant impact. The Aussie machine is running smoothly, and the SCG might just be their red carpet to a 3-0 clean sweep. So, what can India cling to? Positives, yes, there are a few! Rohit is back among runs, Iyer looked solid, and Axar Patel’s late cameos are gold. But the middle order still feels like an untested experiment, and the death bowling - oh boy - still feels like an open wound. Can Siraj and Arshdeep finally deliver with the new ball? Can Washington Sundar’s spin choke the Aussie power hitters? The blueprint is simple - take early wickets, break the partnerships, and don’t let Zampa bowl to the lower order. Easy to say, hard to do! The Aussies, though, won’t ease up! Marsh, Short, and Head at the top can destroy rhythm in ten balls flat. And Connolly - what a find! The young left-hander’s fearless approach has added new muscle to their middle order. Zampa and Starc are their finishing weapons - one spins, one swings, and together, they make chasing look like climbing Everest barefoot. Their biggest advantage? Depth! Even Bartlett and Hazlewood chipped in with key wickets. Now, what about Sydney? Ah, the Sydney Cricket Ground, where history meets unpredictability! The pitch here tends to play true, but under lights, there’s that sneaky turn that spinners love. Winning the toss could give an advantage. Expect a par score around 280-300, and anything below, and the chasing team will fancy their chances. Key battles? Oh, plenty! Rohit vs Starc in the Powerplay - a classic. Kohli (if he fires this time) vs Zampa - chapter infinity of their duel. Axar vs Short - a tactical arm wrestle. And don’t miss Siraj vs Marsh - both men love a fight. Every mini-battle here could shape the big war. So, who has the upper hand? On paper - Australia, no debate. But on heart and hunger - maybe, just maybe, India have one more punch left. The series might be lost, but the pride of more than a billion hearts isn’t. Will it be a clean sweep for the Kangaroos or a poetic redemption for the Men in Blue? Well, as cricket’s old poets would say - Hope, like a late-cut, finds its way through the tiniest gaps.
